axes.mac: the MAC seen for the device (ARP, DHCP, mDNS) is not a stable identity
axes.ip: the address of the device changes or is shared
axes.name: the announced name is missing, generic, slug-like or changes
axes.presence: online/offline pattern says little about what the device is
axes.ports: listening ports are absent, shared or dangerous to probe
axes.services: announced services (mDNS, SSDP) come from another device or only when awake
axes.type: the device type is easy to mistake for another one
axes.path: the attachment point of the device (AP, repeater, switch port) changes or is unknown: topology

behaviors.name: Wi-Fi repeater with MAC translation
behaviors.what: A 3-address repeater swaps the client MAC with its own: the router sees one MAC at several IPs.
behaviors.risk: Announcements and history of the clients are filed on the repeater card; the repeater is typed as a phone.
behaviors.expected: A MAC at several addresses identifies none of them: nothing is filed per MAC, the repeater keeps its own type.
behaviors.observed: Real export (own network, 104 h): the repeater's own MAC answers for 3 phones (4 addresses over time); the MAC is locally administered (private). The same repeater appears, masked, in 3 older reports (0.3.7-0.3.9).

behaviors.name: Repeater or bridge with 4-address frames (transparent)
behaviors.what: ARP shows the real client MACs; the repeater is one more device.
behaviors.risk: None for identity; the same repeater may switch mode after a firmware change and look like the case above.
behaviors.expected: Nothing special: every client keeps its own MAC.
behaviors.observed: Real export (A): the same transparent bridging as the mesh above; two access points typed router with certainty 10 (router 5 against server 4), named after the router integration.

behaviors.name: Mesh node: a client roams and its MAC or IP changes
behaviors.what: A client moving between nodes may get a translated MAC and a new IP; reservations tied to the MAC break.
behaviors.risk: The same phone looks like a new device, or two cards for one device.
behaviors.expected: The card follows the anchors (announced name, DHCP class, history), not the MAC; a change of path alone opens no analysis.
behaviors.observed: Real export (A, 21.7 h): two Ubiquiti access points (lite model) in a mesh with active roaming; every client keeps one MAC and one address, so the roaming is invisible to ARP: the attachment point can only come from the access points themselves (controller, HA tracker attributes or a standard like SNMP/LLDP).

behaviors.name: Sleep proxy (Apple TV, base station) answers for a sleeping Mac
behaviors.what: The proxy answers ARP and mDNS for the sleeping host with the proxy MAC.
behaviors.risk: A sleeping Mac looks online with the MAC and services of the proxy.
behaviors.expected: Same rule as a lent MAC: no card or type is taken from a MAC that answers for several addresses.

behaviors.name: Virtual machines (hypervisor OUI)
behaviors.what: VMs carry the OUI of the hypervisor (Proxmox BC:24:11, VMware 00:50:56 / 00:0C:29, Hyper-V 00:15:5D); the OUI says nothing about the guest.
behaviors.risk: The manufacturer of the MAC is taken as the brand of the device.
behaviors.expected: A virtual OUI is not a brand; the type comes from services and ports.

behaviors.name: Cloned VM with a duplicate MAC
behaviors.what: Two addresses answer with the same MAC after a clone.
behaviors.risk: Looks exactly like a lent MAC; histories of two machines mix.
behaviors.expected: Treated as a MAC at several addresses (nothing filed per MAC); the IP conflict is reported once.

behaviors.name: Containers with macvlan or the host's MAC
behaviors.what: Several addresses answer with the MAC of the host, or each container has its own MAC.
behaviors.risk: Services of containers attributed to the host card (or the reverse).
behaviors.expected: Same rule as a lent MAC.
behaviors.observed: Real report (other network, v0.4.4): one MAC with a single-board-computer OUI answers at 2 addresses (two cards): a host with an alias or container address, or a bridge; not told apart by the data.

behaviors.name: One device on Ethernet and Wi-Fi at the same time
behaviors.what: Two addresses and two MACs, one device (NAS, PC, TV box).
behaviors.risk: Two cards for one device, each with half of the evidence.
behaviors.expected: Same non-generic announced name and host name: candidates for the existing merge of cards; never merged on the MAC.

behaviors.name: VPN or subnet router (routes other networks)
behaviors.what: Addresses of another network are reached through one MAC.
behaviors.risk: Remote hosts attributed to the router.
behaviors.expected: Same rule as a lent MAC; the router is typed by its role.

behaviors.name: Phone with a private MAC per network
behaviors.what: iOS 14+ and Android 10+ use one random MAC per network; it changes if the network is forgotten.
behaviors.risk: The same phone shows up as a new device; the manufacturer of the MAC is unknown.
behaviors.expected: The private MAC is a weak clue for a phone (+1) and never an identity; name and DHCP class decide.

behaviors.name: Phone or laptop that rotates its MAC (daily, every 14 days, per policy)
behaviors.what: Several private MACs for the same card in a few days.
behaviors.risk: Counted as new devices, or merged with another card.
behaviors.expected: Two or more private MACs on one card add to the mobile score; a replaced card with a global MAC does not.

behaviors.name: Phone that announces its name only when awake
behaviors.what: A short scan misses the announcement; the name is known only from the memory.
behaviors.risk: The name falls back to the DHCP host name or the IP.
behaviors.expected: The remembered name stays; a lower-weight new candidate does not replace it.

behaviors.name: Battery IoT that wakes rarely and receives no connections
behaviors.what: No open ports, silent for hours or days.
behaviors.risk: Taken as gone, or as a phone because it has no ports.
behaviors.expected: Absence of ports is a weak clue and never enough; a silent device waits (analysis: «waiting for traffic»), it is not mutated.

behaviors.name: Printer with a raw print port (9100-9107, 515)
behaviors.what: Whatever is sent to the port is printed.
behaviors.risk: An HTTP probe prints sheets of text.
behaviors.expected: Print ports are never probed with HTTP nor version-detected; the type comes from other evidence.

behaviors.name: TV, stick or cast receiver
behaviors.what: Plays video; may use a random-looking MAC or an Android fingerprint (also used by phones).
behaviors.risk: Typed as a phone.
behaviors.expected: Receiving or playing video takes points away from «phone»; the Android fingerprint alone is not enough.

behaviors.name: Fixed PC or TV switched off every evening
behaviors.what: Many online/offline transitions with the manufacturer's MAC.
behaviors.risk: High churn read as a phone.
behaviors.expected: Churn counts only with a private MAC or a recognised laptop.

behaviors.name: Laptop on Wi-Fi (global or private MAC)
behaviors.what: Comes and goes like a phone.
behaviors.risk: Mixed up with a phone or an IoT device.
behaviors.expected: A recognised laptop counts as mobile (the same group as a phone or tablet).

behaviors.name: IP camera (RTSP, ONVIF)
behaviors.what: Always on, several media ports, a web page.
behaviors.risk: Typed as a generic web device.
behaviors.expected: Standard services (RTSP 554, ONVIF) decide the type, never a brand.

behaviors.name: NAS or server with many services
behaviors.what: SMB, web, SSH, DNS on one address.
behaviors.risk: A shared port (445, 53) points at two types.
behaviors.expected: Shared ports give points to every type they can mean; the others decide.

behaviors.name: Device whose address changes (lease or renewal)
behaviors.what: The same MAC answers at a new address.
behaviors.risk: A new card and a lost history.
behaviors.expected: An offline device whose own MAC answers at exactly one other free address is followed there; a lent MAC is never followed.

behaviors.name: Replaced network card (new global MAC)
behaviors.what: Same device and address, new manufacturer MAC.
behaviors.risk: Read as a rotating-MAC phone.
behaviors.expected: A global MAC does not count as rotation.

behaviors.name: IoT announcing a slug name (model-and-hex)
behaviors.what: Names like model-3494547841D9.
behaviors.risk: A raw identifier shown as the name.
behaviors.expected: Slug names are the weakest candidates; a user-chosen name always wins.

behaviors.name: Repeater whose own MAC is locally administered (looks private)
behaviors.what: The lent MAC has the private bit set, so «private MAC» (+1 for phone) applies to the repeater itself.
behaviors.risk: A repeater with some presence flaps or a stray mobile service crosses the phone threshold: it did, 5 points against 3, in the debug export of 2026-10-11.
behaviors.expected: A private MAC and a few flaps stay below the threshold for a device with listening ports; a MAC at several addresses never counts as private.
behaviors.observed: Real export (own network): the repeater scored 2 in production and 5 in debug; the gap was a mobile service announced at a neighbour address.

behaviors.name: Phone that alternates between the AP (own private MAC) and a repeater (lent MAC)
behaviors.what: The card changes MAC many times between two values, with the same name carried along.
behaviors.risk: A flood of «MAC takeover» events (47 in 104 h for one phone) read as identity changes; history and alerts get noisy.
behaviors.expected: A flip between known MACs of the same card (private, or lent) is never a second device (vetoes); it is a change of path.
behaviors.observed: Real export (own network): one phone, 47 changes between its own private MAC and the repeater's; another, 55 changes between the repeater's MAC and a second private one.

behaviors.name: One phone, two cards (two addresses, one private MAC at different times)
behaviors.what: The same private MAC answers at two addresses, never at the same moment.
behaviors.risk: Two cards for one phone, each with half of the history; or, if read as lent, the MAC is ignored altogether.
behaviors.expected: A MAC at two addresses at the SAME time is lent; at different times it is an address change and the old card is followed or merged.
behaviors.observed: Real export (own network): two pairs of cards (same name, same private MAC) on two addresses each.

behaviors.name: Two devices alternating on the same address
behaviors.what: The address answers now with one MAC, now with another, over and over.
behaviors.risk: Noise and mixed attributes: 1211 shadow rows in 21.7 h and, at some changes, the name of one device with the brand of the other.
behaviors.expected: Already so: the module identity_shift judges the two owners as different devices (needs two independent families of evidence, vetoes for private and shared MACs), warns once and changes nothing on the card. Open: the analysis state for the card and a limit to the shadow rows of a contended address.
behaviors.observed: Real export (A): a LTE modem and a camera on one address, 1211 MAC changes in 21.7 h.

behaviors.name: Name says one thing, brand and announced name another
behaviors.what: A name chosen in Home Assistant says «router», the brand is a phone-only maker and mDNS announces «Android».
behaviors.risk: Typed phone with certainty 95 on one anchor, while another anchor says the opposite.
behaviors.expected: Anchors that disagree open an analysis; certainty cannot be high while an anchor contradicts it.
behaviors.observed: Real export (A): a device named as a router by the user, typed phone with certainty 95 because the brand is phone-only.

behaviors.name: Client tracked by a router integration in Home Assistant
behaviors.what: Home Assistant knows the client only as a device_tracker; its device name is the MAC and the title of the integration is the name of the router.
behaviors.risk: Every tracked client is named after the router (11 of 51 cards in one export: a vacuum, a laptop, a phone, two access points).
behaviors.expected: A card known only as a tracker never takes the title of the integration as its name; a real device name or a name chosen by the user is kept.
behaviors.observed: Real export (A): 11 cards of 51 carried the name of the router integration.

behaviors.name: Attachment point unknown (flat network, transparent APs)
behaviors.what: ARP shows every client at the router; which AP or repeater a client sits behind is not in the data.
behaviors.risk: A topology drawn from ARP alone is a guess presented as a fact.
behaviors.expected: Every link carries its source and a confidence; a link without evidence is drawn as unknown, never as certain.
behaviors.observed: Real exports: a lent MAC proves 'behind this repeater' (3 phones behind one repeater); transparent APs prove nothing.

behaviors.name: Solar inverter, battery, meter, wallbox (energy devices)
behaviors.what: The kind «inverter» exists but is recognised only from words in a name, model or title; no standard port or announced service points to it.
behaviors.risk: A real inverter stays generic or plain «iot»: two of three real networks have one (a GoodWe announcing its own service name, a Huawei with no open port and no announcement).
behaviors.expected: Standards first: Modbus TCP (502) as a shared industrial/energy clue with low weight (inverters, meters, wallboxes, PLCs); a device with only a brand and no data stays «generic» and enters analysis, never guessed.
behaviors.observed: Real exports: A (0.5.0) one card announcing a vendor-named mDNS service typed iot with no kind; B (0.6.3) a card known only by its brand, no ports, typed generic.

behaviors.name: Device known only by the maker of its MAC, silent
behaviors.what: No open port, no announcement, no name: only the manufacturer from the MAC, and the maker sells many kinds of devices.
behaviors.risk: A wrong guess from the brand, or a card that stays generic for ever.
behaviors.expected: It stays generic and enters analysis («waiting for traffic»); the user can name it. Never a type from the brand alone.
behaviors.observed: Real export (B): the maker sells phones, routers and inverters; the card is an inverter.

behaviors.name: Small IoT that struggles under a port scan (slow, near the timeout)
behaviors.what: A 1000-port pilot takes 14-16 s on small relays and dimmers, close to the 15 s host timeout; the device may answer late or freeze for a while.
behaviors.risk: The same device is piloted again and again (twice in two minutes in a real export) and may hang.
behaviors.expected: A device found slow is remembered when it is added and never piloted again: targeted ports only, one probe at a time.
behaviors.observed: Real export (B, 0.6.3): 13 of 21 devices slow (13-16 s); the flag learned by the first search was dropped when the devices were added, so the deep search piloted them again.

behaviors.name: PLC, CNC machine or other industrial controller
behaviors.what: Industrial protocols (S7 102, Modbus 502, EtherNet/IP 44818, BACnet 47808...) and firmware that may not tolerate unexpected traffic.
behaviors.risk: An active probe or an OS fingerprint disturbs a machine; or the device is mistaken for a generic server.
behaviors.expected: Industrial protocol ports are never probed beyond a plain connect; no OS or version detection on them; the device is typed from the standard protocol and left alone.

overlaps.risk: A phone behind a repeater: its private MAC is hidden behind the lent one.
overlaps.expected: The phone keeps its class from name and model; the lent MAC adds nothing.

overlaps.risk: A neighbour's mobile service is filed on the repeater (the real case of 2026-10-11).
overlaps.expected: Nothing is filed per lent MAC: the repeater stays a router.

overlaps.risk: A client changes address behind a lent MAC and is «followed» to another one.
overlaps.expected: A MAC at several addresses is never followed.

overlaps.risk: One device on Wi-Fi through the repeater and on Ethernet: three addresses, two MACs.
overlaps.expected: Cards are merged only on name and host name, never on the lent MAC.

overlaps.risk: A TV with a random-looking MAC and an Android fingerprint.
A quiet device with a private MAC and no ports.
overlaps.expected: Private MAC (+1) and no ports (+1) stay below the threshold.

overlaps.risk: A fixed PC with a new NIC, off every night.
overlaps.expected: Not a phone: global MACs do not count as rotation and the churn needs a private MAC.

overlaps.risk: Two clones of one VM on the same hypervisor OUI.
overlaps.expected: The OUI is no brand; the duplicate MAC is treated as shared.

overlaps.risk: A printer asleep: no answer to probes, but a raw port is open when awake.
overlaps.expected: The raw port is still never probed; the device waits for traffic.

overlaps.risk: The repeater (private MAC) plus a neighbour's mobile service: the real case that made it a phone.
overlaps.expected: Nothing is filed under a lent MAC and the private MAC alone stays below the threshold.

overlaps.risk: The phone's flips between its MAC and the lent one are taken as new identities.
overlaps.expected: A lent MAC is never an identity; the flip is a change of path.

overlaps.risk: An address change of a phone with a private MAC is not followed because the MAC looks shared.
overlaps.expected: Shared means at the same time; at different times the card follows the MAC.

overlaps.risk: Same address two MACs (conflict) against same MAC two addresses (duplicate or lent): opposite shapes, easily mixed up.
overlaps.expected: Each shape has its own rule; neither feeds names or brands to a card.
